title: Amazon
description:
The wreck is located on the foreshore close to two outfalls to the south of Aberavon harbour. The main area of wreckage lies close to the most southerly of the outfalls and consists of the lower section of the hull and framing to the turn of the bilge, with the collapsed bow section lying to the north. Another small section of wreckage lies to the south at 51 34 01N, 3 47 31W. Another section of wreckage which may be associated with the wreck lies to the north east, again close to the outfall, at 51 34 07N 3 47 32W (see NPRN 418106). Closeby, a small section protrudes above the sand at 51 34 06N 3 47 30W. Further to the south east, at some distance from the main concentration of wreckage and the outfalls, is another section of wreckage 51 33 53N 3 47 19W, which may be associated with AMAZON (possibly part of the stern).

Event and Historical Information:
The AMAZON was a four-masted iron barque built by Barclay, Curle & Co, Greenock, in 1886 (yard number 342). Technical and configuration specifications are given as 2062gt, 1901nt; 287ft length x 42ft breadth x 12ft 5in depth . The barque had established a record for sailing from Melbourne to Antwerp in 72 days. At time of loss on 1 September 1908, the vessel was owned by Robert Hill of Greenock and was carrying a cargo of coal from Port Talbot to Iquique, Chili, under the command of master Andrew Garrick. The AMAZON had left Port Talbot on the 31 August 1908, but the worsening weather caused the ship anchor in Swansea Bay. By early morning, the wind had reached hurricane force and the anchor cables were unable to take the strain and parted. The ship was blown across Swansea Bay flying the red ensign upside to form the international signal of distress. The vessel ran shore a mile and a half east of the Port Talbot dock entrance. The captain was swept off his feet and dashed unconscious against the deckhouse. He was lashed to a mast by the ship's carpenter. A ship's boat was lowered by was immediately smashed to pieces. The ship's cook was the first to be washed overboard. The remainder of the crew took to the rigging. Attempts to get a line to the ship by rocket apparatus failed, and the Mumbles lifeboat CHARLIE MEDLAND, was unable to get within a mile of the barque once it was aground because the sea was to shallow. As the masts collapsed, the crew were thrown into the sea. When the tide receded the vessel, Henry Care, master of the Port Talbot tug EMILY CHARLOTTE was able to swim out with a line and bring two survivors onshore. Mr Charles Russell, an engineer, managed to rescue another from the rigging. Survivors were taken to Morfa Cottage where they were tended by Dr J H Williams of Aberavon. Those saved were E Halley, first mate and able seamen, John Adams, Sidney Evans, W Nolan, William Wickenberg and John Lockwood. John Lockwood died of pneumonia a few days later. The hull of the ship was sold to Messrs Thomas Ward & Co, Briton Ferry, for £315 and the breaking up commenced on the following Monday. The cargo of coal was disposed of for £25. For a time, special trains were laid on to bring sightseers to see the wreck.

title: Historic Field Boundary Evaluation, Amazon Park, Newton Aycliffe
description: The archaeological evaluation was undertaken over five days between the 29th April and the 3rd May 2013, and involved the excavation of nine trenches positioned across seven of the historic field boundaries which lie within the proposed development site. Seven of the nine trenches showed the construction of the field boundaries to be the same as that recorded within the Historic Hedgerow Survey undertaken by Northern Archaeological Associates in 2012. Two of the trenches, Trenches 5 and 11 have provided additional information with regards to construction methods and possible land use.   Trench 5 was excavated through H30 which was believed to exist as a standing wall but excavation revealed it to be an earthen bank construction with two linear ditches, one on either side of the bank. A sherd of medieval pottery was recovered from within the eastern ditch along with a possibly late medieval or post-medieval shard of glass, potentially dating the ditch to the medieval period.   Within Trench 11 excavation revealed a wide V shaped ditch below the position of the current hedgerow. The size of the ditch possibly indicates that this was a former field boundary that at a later date, once it has silted up, has been replaced with the dense hawthorn. A ditched boundary is more indicative of arable farming as a hedgerow is more effective at separating livestock. This V shaped ditch potentially corresponds to the use of this field within the medieval period as it ties in with the upstanding ridge and furrow cultivation within the field to the south. The addition of a hedgerow at a later date may indicate a shift in the utilization of the landscape towards a pastoral regime.                The results obtained during the present evaluation have added a small amount of additional information regarding two of the hedgerows, H30 and H10, but otherwise have served to back up the conclusions drawn in the Historic Hedgerow Survey (NAA 2012).

title: Hitachi Intercity Express Manufacturing Plant, Amazon Park, Newton Aycliffe
description: Wardell Armstrong Archaeology were commissioned by Merchant Place Developments, on behalf of their client Hitachi, to undertake an archaeological strip, map and sample investigation in advance of construction commencing on the new Hitachi Intercity Express manufacturing plant at Newton Aycliffe, Co. Durham .      The archaeological evaluation was undertaken over 100 days between the 15th of April and 30th of August 2013. The evaluation involved the excavation of two open areas (Area AA1 and AA2), totalling 81973m2 of excavation in total. The earliest features comprised two cremations, situated towards the east of the site with Early Bronze-Age flint tools recovered from the burnt remains of the western most cremation. These were evidently burnt with the individual, carefully gathered and placed with the remains. Other early features were observed on the southwest part of site, and comprised of a series of large re-cut pits, possibly a consequence of small scale prehistoric quarry activity.    The excavation also revealed two Iron-Age / Romano-British settlements and a D-shaped enclosure.

title: Amazonense
description:
The wreck has largely collapsed, but parts still stand 2m above the seabed amongst boulders in 8-16m of water. The four-bladed iron propellor is also reported to lie on the seabed. One of its blades has been broken off. Finds recovered and reported to the Receiver of Wreck include the ship's wheel boss, the emergency steering gear capstan, 3 portholes and 7 glass bottles.

Event and Historical Information:
The AMAZONENSE was an iron steamship built by Oswald, Modaunt & Co, Southampton in 1879. Technical and configuration specifications are given as 1865gt, 1449n; 286ft 7in long x 34ft 7in breadth x 24ft depth; 2 decks, 6 bulkheads, boat deck 16ft; official number 81262. At time of loss, the vessel was owned and operated by the Red Cross Line (R Singlehurst) and registered at Liverpool. The ship was enroute from Liverpool to Lisbon and Para, Brazil, under the command of master H Holgate. After leaving Liverpool, the steamship ran into thick fog in St George's Channel, but continued at full speed without use of a lead and line. Due to a defective compass and the crew were unaware of how close the vessel was to land, and the AMAZON ENSE ran ashore on the rocks on the north side of Saint David's Head, 1mile east of Porth-gwyn. It proved impossible to save the vessel and it was sold where it lay, for a very small sum. At the BOT Inquiry held at Liverpool the following month, the Captain was found guilty of failing to use the lead and line, or reduce speed, and his certificate was suspended for three months.

title: Maripasoula (Guyane), Parc amazonien de Guyane, archéologie participative lors de la mission "Mitaraka", rapport de prospection
description:
Cette prospection pédestre archéologique s’est avérée fructueuse avec 8 sites archéologiques et quelques indices de site. Parmi les sites on dénombre 4 sites aménagés dont un site à enclos ou montagne couronnée.
Sur une surface prospectée d’environ 11 km² nous avons effectivement trouvé un élément archéologique par km² ce qui confirme ce chiffre de densité de présence humaine en milieu forestier tropical. Seules plus de datations radiocarbones pourront donner une première date ou fourchette chronologique à ces sites trouvés dans le sud de la Guyane, zone qui semble habitée depuis fort longtemps !

title: AMCR C-201446891A – Dobrovíz, plošný odkryv (2014-06-20 – 2015-03-06)
description:
Fieldwork recorded in the AMCR system.
Finds deposition: ARÚ Praha - Závist.
Location/circumstances: JZ okraj obce, podél železniční trati. Distribuční centrum Amazon.
Description: V rámci záchranného výzkumu v Dobrovízi r. 2014 bylo skryto a prozkoumáno několik ploch: 1 - parkoviště, 2 - čistička odpadních vod, 3 - příjezdová cesta, 4 - plocha haly a zázemí firmy Amazon ("Za tratí"), 5 - liniový výkop podél silnice. Odkryto bylo 470 zahloubených objektů, převážnou většinu z nich tvořily kůlové jamky sídliště ze starší doby bronzové. Odkryty byly rovněž tři hroby z téhož období, tři hroby kultury se šnůrovou keramikou, 3 polozemnice řivnáčské kultury, sídlištní jáma a hliník téže kultury. Dvě sídlištní jámy obsahovaly keramiku michelské kultury, jedna jáma (hliník?) byla datována do jordánovské kultury. Odkryto bylo dále několik desítek kůlových jamek pravěkého stáří, dvě cesty možná již z pozdního středověku/novověku s několik fragmentů pecí se struskou.

title: Roman building debris from Flint...
description: Roman building debris from Flint Hall reported in 1948, although the details are scant and have not been confirmed. Field investigation in 1974 noted a fragment of a probable tegulae tile embedded in a wall at Amazon Farm (formerly Flint Hall Farm) and Medieval tile and sherds together with small fragments of possible Roman tegulae and imbrex in ploughsoil. The amount of material, however, did not form a sufficient concentration to indicate a building site.

title: LORETO
description: "Summary: The wreck of a Peruvian river gunboat which foundered off the Isles of Scilly in 1903, while crossing the Atlantic from Liverpool to be delivered to her new Peruvian owners via the Amazon in Brazil. She is said to have sprung a leak 40 miles NW of the Isles of Scilly, but may have altered her position by the time she sank an hour later. A new vessel, constructed of metal, she was powered by engines."

title: Unnamed Wreck (Mulberry Habrour Phoenix Unit?)
description: Remains comprising square stone/concrete blocks, concrete and wooden or metal piles (?). Possibly associated wth the wreck of the AMAZON (NPRN 274172) or the remains of a terminus for a formal outfall? An alternative identity is offered by T Bennett - the remains of a World War II Mulberry Harbour Phoenix Unit. The remains of a Cromwell tank is reported to be visible at very low tides. The tank was being used to simulate Normandy beachhead landings when it sank into soft sand.  WWW resources: Bennett, T, 2017, Wrecks on Welsh Beaches: Shipwrecks for Walkers, E-book  https://books.google.co.uk/books?id=7Vz5DQAAQBAJ&printsec=frontcover&source=gbs_ge_summary_r&cad=0£v=onepage&q&f=false  Maritime Officer, RCAHNW, January 2018.

title: IRISBROOK
description: "Summary: 1911 wreck of Scottish cargo vessel which foundered 4 miles SSW of the Royal Sovereign Light Vessel after a collision with the VILLE DE BORDEAUX, en route from Swansea via London to Manaus and/or other ports on the River Amazon, with coal, patent fuel, and general cargo. Constructed of steel in 1902, she was a screw-driven steamer. \n\nThe remains of the IRISBROOK are believed to be located at 1599068. The wreck of the IRISBROOK was formerly thought to be located at 911897, but this site has now been amended to 'dead'. The VILLE DE BORDEAUX was also lost in the collision (see 1172755 for the wreck event, and 911498 for the probable remains of the VILLE DE BORDEAUX)."

title: Gidy, zone d'activité (1ère phase) (Loiret-Centre), rapport de diagnostic
description:
La présente intervention constitue la tranche 1 de l’agrandissement de la « Z.A.C du Champ Rouge ». L’ensemble des deux tranches opérationnelles couvrent plus d’une trentaine d’hectares au nord des actuelles plate-formes des entreprises « Deret » et « Amazon ». L’actuel diagnostic a eu pour objectif de caractériser la présence et l’étendue de vestiges archéologiques sur une bande linéaire de 60 m de large (superficie d’emprise d’opération : 24025 m2), destinée à accueillir une extension des entrepôts de la société « Amazon ». L’emprise du présent diagnostic est située au niveau de la limite communale entre Gidy et Saran (limite fixée par la rue des vergers en partie) et à 150 m au nord d’un enclos gaulois (La Tène) perçu lors des opérations précédentes (diagnostic Inrap, 2006, phase 2, enclos n° 9). Ce diagnostic a permis de mettre au jour une petite partie (90 m de large) d’une occupation rurale gallo-romaine, datée entre la fin du Ier et le IIIème siècle inclus et perçue sur trois phases distinctes
d’occupation. Les éléments découverts permettent d’établir deux constats. D’une part, les différents niveaux de remblais d’assainissement mis au jour permettent d’attester des tentatives d’aménagement de zones d’occupations sur des niveaux humides. Ce constat tend à prouver que la nature hydromorphique de ces terrains a toujours procuré de fortes contraintes techniques aux occupants du site. Les structures correspondant à la dernière phase d’occupation (phase 3) sont fortement arasées et difficilement repérables dans des conditions d’interventions hivernales. Les structures relatives aux phases antérieures sont mieux conservées, scellées par les niveaux de remblais. Les vestiges découverts sont interprétables comme des éléments caractéristiques de cour ou d’arrière-cour (cellier, ensilage). L’orientation générale des vestiges tend à prouver que le site et donc les parties d’habitation se développent vers le nord, hors emprise. Par conséquent, il est fort probable que la pars urbana soit découverte lors de la réalisation de la tranche 2 du diagnostic de ces terrains comprenant les 30 hectares situés en bordure nord de cette opération.

title: Other BOX
description:
An incomplete Post Medieval tagua snuff box dating from the late 18th-19th century. The box is of composite construction made from four sections of tagua nut with an iron hinge. The box is decorated with a scene depicting a pitched roof building (brick?) with a central figure of a right facing lady standing holding a book or closed fan and a left facing man siting under a tree holding a mug. The back and sides are decorated with a radiating foliate design possibly tobacco leaves with a central rosette. The side end caps are missing.
Dimensions: length: 63.92mm; width: 30.12mm; thickness: 19.88mm; weight: 43.29mm
The "palm ivory" from the Amazon rainforest bear fruit whose pulpit inner (endosperm) becomes very hard when dry and texture very similar to ivory. It is this which is called vegetable ivory or tagua. The tagua nut carves, turns, polishes easily and almost as finely as ivory. The tagua nut was worked by the sailors who made ​​such small boxes, snuff graters or tobacco also made ​​by convicts. The latter worked to pass the time but mainly to get some money to improve their lives. Can also be attributed to sailors during their long journeys.

title: Copper alloy STRAP FITTING
description:
Cast copper alloy complex petal or cruciform strap junction.  The object is symmetrical.  Two petals are linked together by a central ?amazon shield motif with a shallow horizontal central groove.  The terminals of the shields slightly overlay the base of the petals, creating a crescent shaped panel within the body of the petals.  These panels are subdivided into three 'leaves' containing a blue-turquoise enamel, and the recesses surrounding containing a greenish enamel.  The shield is flanked by two bulls eye motifs (ring-within-a-ring), which inturn are flanked by two rectangular panels.  The rectangular panels are subdivided into four smaller rectangular cells, two containing blue-turquoise enamel, and two containing a greenish enamel.  A rectangular strap bar joins the rectangular panels on the reverse, and consequently when the object is viewed from the front, the strap bar is completely hidden. 
 
  By definition this object is not technically a strap junction, having only one rectangular strap bar on the reverse, however its design and decoration bears close parallels to a number of examples from the 'ring with concealed bars', and 'petal or cruciform' strap junction groupings (cf. MacGregor, p32).  The reverse technology of this artefact is identical to two others noted by MacGregor (1976), both from the petal or cruciform group, found at West Stowe (MacGregor, Vol 2, #28) and Traprain Law (MacGregor, Vol 1, p34).

title: A66 Symmetry Park, Darlington, County Durham
description: Archaeological evaluation trenching was required prior to the construction of an employment park to the west of the A66 on the eastern side of Darlington in County Durham (National Grid Reference NZ 32455 15096). The investigation was commissioned by Prospect Archaeology on behalf of Tritax Symmetry and forms part of the 35ha site granted outline planning permission under reference 07/00041/OUT.   The archaeological evaluation comprised 20 x 100m trenches. Several of these had to be shortened due to ground water (Trenches 4, 7, 8, 9, 11 & 12), the Amazon Distribution Hub's northern property boundary (Trenches 14, 16 & 18), and a modern drainage ditch along the western part of the site (Trenches 1 & 17). The archaeological investigations undertaken on the A66 Symmetry Park site at Darlington, County Durham comprised the excavation of 20 trenches. Geological deposits, undated gullies and subsoil, post-medieval field boundaries, furrows and a pit as well as modern made ground and plough soil were encountered during the works.   These were assigned to four phases of activity: Phase 1: Superficial geological deposits were encountered within all trenches; Phase 2: Three undated gullies within Trench 14 and subsoil within Trenches 3-5, 7, 8, 11-13, 16, 17 and 20; Phase 3: Field boundaries Trench 11, 14 and 15; a pit in Trench 11 and plough furrows within Trenches 5, 11, 12, 15, 19 and 20; and Phase 4: Modern made ground within Trenches 1-4, 7-10 and 16-17 as well as topsoil/plough soil that formed the uppermost deposits within all Trenches.  In terms of addressing the Regional Research priorities there were no prehistoric or Roman archaeological remains identified. The features recorded in the main are related to the agricultural use of the site during the post-medieval period.

title: A66 Employment Park, Darlington: Post-excavation Assessment
description: The original project design for the archaeological evaluation included the investigation of 56 100m long trenches extending across the entire proposed development area. The evaluation was subsequently reduced to 36 trenches covering the Phase 1 development area, the site of the Amazon distribution centre, which occupied the southern half of the development site and an access road along the western margin.  Due to time constraints for the proposed development, work proceeded straight to further mitigation in the form of a strip, map and record excavation. Overburden in the southern part of the site was stripped by machine across an irregular-shaped area covering some 1.7 hectares, with maximum dimensions of 180m east-west and 140m north-south. Machining ceased to the north, east and west as archaeological features petered out, however intense activity did continue to the south of the investigated area. As this area did not form part of the Phase 1 construction, archaeological features in this part of the site were left in situ. An irregular shaped area around a pole carrying a live electricity line within the central southern part of the main excavation area could not be stripped of plough soil.  A c. 0.60m-wide electricity cable trench was excavated under archaeological supervision along the edge of the hedge line forming the southern boundary of the site. Numerous linear features were recorded in section in the part of the cable trench to the south of the SMR area. The purpose of the Strip, Map and Record methodology was to provide a permanent record of all archaeological deposits, features and finds within the identified area prior to their removal through development. Without a more detailed understanding of the date and nature of the archaeological resource present on the site, the identification of specific research objectives is difficult. The Research Framework for the North-East region (Petts & Gerrard 2006) provides guidance on research agendas and is referenced below using the relevant Research Priority code (e.g. Rv).  The excavation of the site was able to relatively date a complex sequence of intercutting linear ditches and other features. The examination of finds recovered from their fills can identify three main phases of human occupation and use above the natural substratum of glacial till (Phase 1). Phase 2. Probable Middle or late Iron Age isolated roundhouse. No finds whatsoever were recovered from the fills associated with it. Phase 3. Roman farmsteads. Two main groups Phase 3.1 and Phase 3.2) of ditch alignments were visible in the west part of the site. The finds from the fills of both Phase 3.1 and Phase 3.2 features are broadly late Roman (3rd and 4th century). However, there is a concentration of earlier sherds in the south-west corner of the site and much more very late Roman material from the central and eastern are of the site. Phase 4. Medieval ridge and furrow field systems  A large assemblage of handmade pottery indicates local supply, common to sites in the region dating from the late Iron Age onwards. The small finds assemblage includes only a few items of significance. These, especially the brooches, are more commonly associated with a Roman-style personal adornment. Nene Valley and Crambeck pottery was also recovered. It is probable that these items and pottery were being acquired using local markets, probably at Piercebridge to the west.  The Phase 2 roundhouse appears to be isolated within an agricultural landscape. Linear ditches appear to have been dug as field boundaries and drove ways, some of which appear to respect the entranceway in the roundhouse drainage ditch leading to the house itself.
